terms.definition: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea: teacher, school, book, freedom.
terms.asl: Some ASL nouns and verbs share a handshape but differ in movement. The noun often uses a short, repeated movement (CHAIR) while the verb uses one longer movement (SIT).

terms.definition: A word for an action or state: run, eat, think, be.
terms.asl: Many ASL verbs move between locations in space to show who does what to whom. These are called directional or indicating verbs (for example GIVE or HELP).

terms.definition: A word that describes a noun: big, red, happy.
terms.asl: Adjectives can come before or after the noun in ASL, and facial expression often shows how much (a little big versus very big).

terms.definition: A word that describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb, often telling how, when or how much: quickly, yesterday, very.
terms.asl: ASL often shows manner by changing the verb's movement and the signer's face instead of adding a separate sign. Signing WORK with a tense, repeated movement can mean working hard.

terms.definition: The small words a, an and the, which come before nouns.
terms.asl: ASL has no signs for a, an or the. To point out a specific person or thing, signers point to it or to a place in space (an index point).

terms.definition: A word that stands in for a noun: I, you, she, they, it.
terms.asl: ASL pronouns are made by pointing: at yourself for I or ME, at the other person for YOU, or at a spot in space that you have set up for someone who is not present.

terms.definition: A word that shows position or relationship: in, on, under, with, to.
terms.asl: ASL has signs like IN and ON, but location is often shown directly by placing classifier handshapes in space.

terms.definition: A word that joins words or ideas: and, but, or, because.
terms.asl: "And" is usually not signed. Ideas are joined by pauses, body shifts or listing on the fingers of the non-dominant hand.

terms.definition: The person or thing doing the action in a sentence. In "Maria reads," Maria is the subject.
terms.asl: Subjects are often set up first or understood from context, and pronoun subjects may be dropped once it is clear who is being talked about.

terms.definition: The person or thing that receives the action. In "Maria reads a book," book is the object.
terms.asl: Objects are often moved to the front of the sentence as the topic, marked with raised eyebrows.

terms.definition: The verb form that shows when something happens: walk, walked, will walk.
terms.asl: ASL verbs do not change for tense. A time sign such as YESTERDAY or TOMORROW, usually at the start of the sentence, sets the time until it changes.

terms.definition: A complete thought with a subject and a verb.
terms.asl: A common ASL order is time first, then the topic, then the comment: YESTERDAY STORE I GO.

terms.definition: A way of writing signs with English words in capital letters, such as STORE I GO. A gloss names the sign; it is not a translation.
terms.asl: Hyphens between letters (J-A-Y) mean the word is fingerspelled.

terms.definition: Spelling a word letter by letter with the manual alphabet.
terms.asl: Used for names, places, brand names and words without a common sign. Keep the hand steady in one spot, usually near the shoulder of your dominant side.

terms.definition: The shape the hand makes during a sign, such as a flat B hand or a fist A hand.
terms.asl: Handshape is one of the parameters of a sign. Changing only the handshape can turn one sign into another.

terms.definition: Which way the palm faces: out, in toward you, up, down or to the side.
terms.asl: Fingerspelled letters usually face out toward the person watching.

terms.definition: Where a sign is made: at the forehead, chin, chest, in neutral space in front of the body, and so on.
How the hands move during a sign. On the cards, red arrows show movement and faded hands show where the movement starts.
The building blocks of a sign: handshape, palm orientation, location, movement and non-manual markers. Change any one and you can get a different sign.
Grammar shown with the face, head and body instead of the hands: eyebrows, mouth shape, head tilt or shake.
terms.asl: Raised eyebrows mark yes/no questions and topics. Lowered, furrowed eyebrows mark wh-questions. A head shake can make a sentence negative.

terms.definition: A sentence structure where you name the topic first, then say something about it.
terms.asl: BOOK (eyebrows raised), I READ FINISH. means "I already read the book."

terms.definition: A question asking who, what, where, when, why, which or how.
terms.asl: The question sign often comes at the end, with eyebrows lowered: YOUR NAME WHAT?

terms.definition: A question that can be answered with yes or no.
terms.asl: Shown by raising the eyebrows and tilting the head slightly forward, often through the whole question: YOU DEAF?

terms.definition: A handshape that stands for a type of object (a car, a person, a flat surface) and shows how it moves or where it is.
terms.asl: A 3 handshape lying on its side can show a car driving uphill, parking or swerving.

terms.definition: The hand you sign with most, usually your writing hand. It does the movement in one-handed signs.
terms.asl: The figure on these cards signs with the right hand. Left-handed signers mirror everything.
